newsitem.title: USA: Clinton criticizes Republican comp time bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton criticizes Republican comp time bill.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday renewed his threat to veto a Republican bill allowing employees to take time off in lieu of overtime pay, charging it eroded vital labour laws and could hurt working families.

In his weekly radio address, Clinton said if Republicans were serious about helping hard-pressed working parents they should expand the 1993 Family and Medical Leave Act, which allows employees to take time off without pay.
He also called on Congress to adopt a different version of comp time legislation he has endorsed that includes more stringent labour safeguards.
"Strong comp time legislation would give employees the choice of when they take time off. That's the best way to strengthen families and to give parents more flexibility," Clinton said.
"But under the congressional (Republican) plan, employees who take comp time could be forced to work extra hours at night or on the weekend to make up the time without any overtime pay," he said.

Clinton wrote to House Speaker Newt Gingrich last week threatening to veto the bill. The Republican legislation is vehemently opposed by organised labour, which gave millions of dollars to the Democratic party in the 1996 elections.
The House Thursday passed the Working Families Flexibility Act on a party line vote of 222-210.

Republican leaders have made the legislation a top priority in an effort to show they are sensitive to the needs of working mothers, who were cool to their party in the recent campaign. It also has the strong support of business.
The bill would let private businesses give their workers the choice of taking 1-1/2 hours of paid time off instead of time-and-a-half pay, for every hour of overtime worked.
It amends a 1938 labour law requiring overtime pay for most employees who work more than 40 hours a week. Public sector employees already have the ability to opt for comp time.
About 57 percent of the U.S. work force, or 68 million employees, are hourly workers who would be affected by the Republican measure.
Senate leaders hope to take up a similar bill soon, but could be blocked by Democrats.

House Republicans angrily deny charges that workers would be subject to abuse under the bill. They said they had built in protections to ensure employers did not coerce employees into taking take comp time or punish any who wanted overtime.

Any comp time agreement would have to be voluntary and workers could withdraw from such arrangements. Accrued comp time not used would be cashed out each year and workers could sue for damages if employers did not follow the law.
Democrats said the bill would let employers deny a request for comp time if it would disrupt business, making it likely that workers would work overtime without receiving time off.
The House bill allows up to 160 hours of comp time to accrue each year, which labour leaders call a short-term loan from workers to employers.
Clinton has recommended expanding the Family and Medical Leave law to let workers take time off for such things as a teacher conference or a child's medical checkup.

"Congress should pass expanded family leave and a strong comp time bill. The moment a responsible comp time bill hits my desk I will gladly sign it. It will be good for workers, good for business, good for the economy and strong in the building of our families," Clinton said.
"But let me also be clear: I will have to veto any legislation that fails to guarantee real choice for employees," he said.
